extracted.subtask_description: Advice for novelists on creating sustained, character-driven fiction: how to originate stories, inhabit characters, control language, structure plots and dialogue, and avoid common faults such as episodic digressions and tedium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin only when you have a story to tell
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist should commence his novel not because he has to tell a story, but because he has a story to tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first novel generally springs from a genuine cause (a series of events or development of character) that 'tickles your fancy or moves your pathos.' By contrast, writing subsequent novels out of obligation or habit leads to cudgelling of the brain and often produces work that distresses the audience. Avoid starting fiction merely to supply output or because of commercial/professional pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain continuous observation and reception
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist must continue the work of observation and reception in all walks of life; if he 'shuts his eyes and shuts his ears' his power fades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The material that feeds fiction is accumulated unconsciously through living actively in the world. This intake is labour (even when unconscious) and must be ongoing—not only at the desk but in intercourse with others—else characters and scenes lose freshness and become wooden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live with and know characters intimately
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist must be able to 'live with' his fictitious personages: hate them, love them, argue with them, know their depths and limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intimacy with characters means knowing tone of voice, expressions, likely words and reactions. Without such constant companionship with one's characters the writer cannot make them speak, move, and live as human creatures to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track character change and time consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should show change over time; 'On the last day of each month recorded, every person in his novel should be a month older than on the first.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be consistent about the passage of time and note every change. This encourages verisimilitude and prevents static 'toy' characters. Temporal attention to detail reinforces the sense that characters live and age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pleasant, intelligible, and harmonious language
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist's language must be pleasant: intelligible without trouble and harmonious to the ear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers can reject a novelist for poor style even when other gifts exist. More than mere correctness is required: language should conduct the writer's meaning to the reader with clarity and pleasing rhythm. Pleasantness matters because novel-reading is elective, not a duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for pellucid clarity of meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaning must be 'so pellucid that the meaning should be rendered without an effort of the reader'—not something which must be hammered out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid doubtful collocations and stumbling-block passages. A severe self-critique habit will help remove any phrase that forces the reader to stop and puzzle out the sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate harmonious prose rhythm by training the ear
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmony in prose comes from practice of the ear; the writer should learn to weigh the rhythm of every word as it falls from his pen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarity with metrical forms and musical sensibility helps. The writer should train to appreciate metrical duration of syllables so that prose reads with natural rhythm; this habit charms readers even if they cannot say why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude episodes; make every sentence serve the story
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be no episodes in a novel: 'Every sentence, every word, through all those pages, should tend to the telling of the story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodes and digressions distract and irritate readers. Exclusion of episodes must extend into smallest details—sentences and words that do not serve the main story ought to be cut or refocused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use subsidiary plots only insofar as they elucidate the main story
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel may have many parts or subsidiary plots, but these must 'all tend to the elucidation of the main story' and be part of one cohesive work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may enlarge a plot to occupy required length, but subsidiary material should not read as separate pictures; it should reinforce and clarify the principal narrative rather than distract from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage novel length by proportion; suit scope to subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Though long form is often required, the novelist must study proportion so that the story naturally fills the required space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may be contracted to fixed lengths (three volumes or magazine pages); learning to adapt subject to canvas without digressing requires practice in proportion and structuring, not mere padding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make dialogue serve the main story; avoid discursive conversations
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue is agreeable only so long as it 'tends in some way to the telling of the main story'; long extraneous conversations will make the reader feel cheated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers sense when a dialogue deviates from the story even if they can't point to the moment. Avoid using conversations as opportunities for unrelated literary, political or philosophical digression that stalls narrative momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render dialogue true to situation: balance realism and correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Put into characters' mouths such words 'as persons so situated would probably use'—steer between pedantic correctness and slavish, offensive inaccuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fully realistic transcription of ordinary talk can seem graceless or grotesque; overly correct speech appears unreal. The novelist must create the auditory impression of reality while keeping readability and artistic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer short speeches; avoid long monologues unless justified
rubrics_metrics.description: No character should utter much above a dozen words at a breath—unless longer speech is justified by the occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary talk tends to short, sharp sentences, often incomplete. Keeping speeches concise sustains realism and pace; long floods of speech need strong justification to avoid boring or unconvincing dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let human nature be your guide (but write with art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human nature must guide the novelist; even where effective exceptions exist, following human nature is generally the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers who appreciate human nature will still demand artistic ability and literary aptitude; portrayals that defy human nature can succeed only rarely and usually as exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire knowledge of human nature through listening, observing, and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of what men and women would say and do must be acquired by constant and intelligent practice—by listening and carrying manners away in memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like a compositor learning his trade, the novelist needs habitual, attentive observation of life so as to write convincingly about people in particular positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against tedium; heed when the work feels long
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid creating tedium at book, chapter, passage, or paragraph level; the writer's own feeling that 'the thing is becoming long' is usually the best warning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tedium is contagious: if the writer is bored or thinks the work is becoming long, readers will likely feel the same. Be self-aware and cut or tighten where the story flags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be a severe self-critic; eliminate stumbling-blocks
rubrics_metrics.description: The habit of writing clearly comes to the writer who is a severe critic to himself; he should leave no doubtful passage behind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even small doubtful collocations can act as stumbling-blocks. Revise ruthlessly to ensure every phrase conveys precisely the sense intended without causing the reader to stumble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation and mannerism in style; choose good models
rubrics_metrics.description: Affectation disfigures otherwise good style; mannerism and artificial conceits are faults to be avoided—do not imitate such mannerisms (e.g., Dickens' jerky ungrammatical style) blindly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study good models (the author recommends Thackeray's clear, harmonious style) rather than copying the mannerisms or comic devices of successful popular writers; imitation of mannerisms can do harm and create poor imitators.
